questions.question: Which Spaniard is credited with inventing the modern mop with a wringer bucket?
questions.fact: Manuel Jalón, an aeronautical engineer, developed the "fregona" in Zaragoza in the 1950s, sparing people from scrubbing floors on their knees.

questions.question: Which Catalan businessman launched the Chupa Chups lollipop in 1958?
questions.fact: The name comes from the Spanish verb "chupar", to suck. Bernat reportedly wanted a sweet children could eat without getting sticky fingers.

questions.question: Which Spanish engineer built the "Telekino", an early radio remote control, in 1903?
questions.fact: In 1906 he steered a boat by radio in Bilbao harbour, in front of a large crowd that included King Alfonso XIII.

questions.question: Isaac Peral, from Cartagena, designed a pioneering electric-powered what?
questions.fact: Launched in Cádiz in 1888, Peral's submarine was never adopted by the navy. Today it is displayed in Cartagena's Naval Museum.

questions.question: Which Catalan inventor built the "Ictíneo" submarines in Barcelona in the mid-1800s?
questions.fact: Ictíneo II used an early air-independent engine: a chemical reaction that heated its boiler and released oxygen for the crew.

questions.question: Which Spanish engineer designed the cable car that still carries tourists over the Niagara whirlpool?
questions.fact: It opened in 1916. In 1912 he also built "El Ajedrecista", a machine that could play a simple chess endgame by itself.

questions.question: Which game did Alejandro Finisterre patent in Spain in 1937?
questions.fact: By his own account, he dreamed up "futbolín" for children injured in the Civil War. Similar games had been patented earlier in other countries.

questions.question: Which device for looking at the vocal cords did Spanish singing teacher Manuel García invent?
questions.fact: García reportedly worked it out in 1854 using a dentist's mirror and sunlight. He went on to live to the age of 101.

questions.question: The oldest surviving camera photograph, from around 1826, was taken by which Frenchman?
questions.fact: It shows the view from his window in Burgundy and needed an exposure of many hours, possibly even days.

questions.question: Johannes Gutenberg is famous for developing what in Europe around 1440?
questions.fact: His most famous book, the Gutenberg Bible, was printed in the 1450s. Fewer than 50 copies are known to survive, some incomplete.

questions.question: Thomas Edison's lab produced a long-lasting version of which invention in 1879?
questions.fact: Edison didn't do it alone: Joseph Swan made a working bulb in England around the same time, and they later merged into "Ediswan".

questions.question: Which device did Edison invent in 1877 that could record and play back sound?
questions.fact: The first words he recorded were reportedly "Mary had a little lamb". The flat-disc gramophone came later, from Emile Berliner.

questions.question: Which appliance was reportedly inspired when a radar engineer's chocolate bar melted in his pocket?
questions.fact: Percy Spencer worked for Raytheon. Its first microwave, the 1947 "Radarange", stood about 1.8 m tall and weighed around 340 kg.

questions.question: Which sticky invention grew out of a "failed", super-weak glue made at 3M?
questions.fact: Spencer Silver made the glue in 1968. Colleague Art Fry found a use for it: stopping his bookmarks falling out of his church hymn book.

questions.question: What inspired Swiss engineer George de Mestral to invent Velcro?
questions.fact: The name combines the French words "velours" (velvet) and "crochet" (hook), after the soft loop side and the hooked side.

questions.question: Who invented dynamite and later used his fortune to fund famous prizes?
questions.fact: Reportedly, a newspaper mistook his brother's death for his in 1888 and called him "the merchant of death", which may have pushed him to create the prizes.

questions.question: Superglue was first stumbled upon in World War II while trying to make what?
questions.fact: Harry Coover rejected it as far too sticky. He rediscovered it in 1951, and it went on sale in 1958 as "Eastman 910".

questions.question: Who is credited with the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796?
questions.fact: Jenner used material from cowpox sores. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin "vacca", meaning cow.

questions.question: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.fact: One of his first X-ray images showed his wife's hand, wedding ring and all. She reportedly said, "I have seen my death."

questions.question: James Watt is famous for greatly improving which machine?
questions.fact: Watt coined the term "horsepower" to compare his engines with the horses they were replacing.

questions.question: Who built the first electric battery, the "voltaic pile", in 1800?
questions.fact: It was a stack of zinc and copper discs separated by cloth soaked in salt water. The unit "volt" is named after him.

questions.question: Which US Founding Father invented the lightning rod and is credited with bifocals?
questions.fact: Franklin also invented the "glass armonica", an instrument of spinning glass bowls that Mozart composed music for.

questions.question: Which Swedish-American engineer developed the modern zip in 1913?
questions.fact: The name "zipper" came from the B.F. Goodrich company, which used it in the 1920s for rubber boots that fastened with one.

questions.question: The ballpoint pen, often called a "biro", is named after an inventor from which country?
questions.fact: László Bíró was a journalist who noticed how fast newspaper ink dried. He later moved to Argentina, where his pen took off in the 1940s.

questions.question: Which Italian pioneered long-distance radio, sending a signal across the Atlantic in 1901?
questions.fact: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with the German Karl Ferdinand Braun for their work on wireless telegraphy.

questions.question: Which Scot gave the first public demonstration of television, in London in 1926?
questions.fact: Baird's mechanical system used a spinning disc. The BBC dropped it in 1937 in favour of fully electronic television.

questions.question: Who invented the first commercially successful dishwasher, patented in 1886?
questions.fact: Cochrane, a wealthy American, reportedly wanted a machine that washed faster than her servants and stopped them chipping her china.

questions.question: Hollywood star Hedy Lamarr co-patented which wartime invention?
questions.fact: Her 1942 patent with composer George Antheil aimed to stop radio-guided torpedoes being jammed, using a piano-roll-style mechanism.

questions.question: In 1903 Mary Anderson patented which car accessory?
questions.fact: She reportedly got the idea on a snowy tram ride in New York, watching the driver lean out of the window to clear the glass.

questions.question: Paper was invented in which country?
questions.fact: Tradition credits a court official called Cai Lun around AD 105, although older scraps of paper have since been found in China.

questions.question: Paper, printing and the compass are three of ancient China's "four great inventions". What is the fourth?
questions.fact: Gunpowder was reportedly discovered by Chinese alchemists searching for an elixir of eternal life, around the 9th century.

questions.question: The first known patent application for a telescope was made in 1608 in which country?
questions.fact: Galileo didn't invent the telescope, but after hearing about it in 1609 he built his own and was among the first to turn one to the sky.

questions.question: The sandwich is named after an 18th-century English earl. What was his title?
questions.fact: Legend says John Montagu ate beef between bread so he could keep gambling. One biographer thinks it was more likely at his desk.

questions.question: In 1873 Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented work trousers strengthened with what?
questions.fact: Davis was a tailor in Nevada who had the idea. He teamed up with Strauss, a cloth merchant, because he couldn't afford the patent fee.

questions.question: Which everyday object did Walter Hunt patent in 1849?
questions.fact: He reportedly invented it to pay off a 15-dollar debt, then sold the patent for 400 dollars, missing out on a fortune.

questions.question: Which super-strong fibre, used in bulletproof vests, did chemist Stephanie Kwolek invent?
questions.fact: Kwolek made the breakthrough at DuPont in 1965. Weight for weight, Kevlar is said to be about five times stronger than steel.

questions.question: Which non-stick coating was discovered by accident in 1938 during research into fridge gases?
questions.fact: Roy Plunkett at DuPont found that a gas cylinder had mysteriously turned its contents into a slippery white powder.

questions.question: Pasteurisation, heating food to kill germs, is named after which scientist?
questions.fact: Pasteur first used it in the 1860s to stop wine and beer going off, long before it became standard for milk.

questions.question: Which doctor's tool did René Laennec invent in 1816?
questions.fact: His first one was reportedly a rolled-up paper tube, used because he felt awkward putting his ear to a young woman's chest.

questions.question: Which English scientist built the first electric motor and dynamo in the 1820s and 1830s?
questions.fact: Faraday had little schooling: he started as a bookbinder's apprentice and taught himself science by reading the books he bound.

questions.question: Which inventor, born in today's Croatia, developed the AC induction motor?
questions.fact: The scientific unit of magnetic field strength, the tesla, is named after him, and so is the electric car company.

questions.question: What does a patent give an inventor?
options: Exclusive rights for a limited time
A free licence to sell abroad
questions.fact: In most countries, including Spain, a patent lasts up to 20 years from filing. After that, anyone can use the invention.

questions.question: What was the first product scanned with a barcode at a shop till, in 1974?
questions.fact: By his own account, inventor Joseph Woodland got the idea by drawing Morse code dots and dashes in beach sand and stretching them into lines.

questions.question: Which code of dots and dashes is named after a US painter turned inventor?
questions.fact: Samuel Morse was a successful portrait painter. The first long-distance telegraph message, in 1844, was "What hath God wrought".

questions.question: At about what age did Louis Braille create his reading system for blind people?
questions.fact: Blinded as a small child in an accident in his father's workshop, he based his system on a military "night writing" code.

questions.question: Which German company first sold aspirin, in 1899?
questions.fact: Willow bark, which contains a related chemical, had been used against pain and fever since ancient times.

questions.question: Which toy was invented after a naval engineer watched a spring fall off a shelf and "walk"?
questions.fact: Richard James was reportedly working on springs to steady ship instruments. His wife Betty found the name "Slinky" in a dictionary.

questions.question: Play-Doh was first sold as what?
questions.fact: It became a toy in the 1950s after a nursery teacher found that children loved modelling with the cleaning putty.

questions.question: Bubble wrap was originally invented in 1957 as what?
questions.fact: Its inventors then tried selling it as greenhouse insulation, before IBM began using it to protect computers being shipped.

questions.question: Which breakfast cereal came from the Kellogg brothers' accidental discovery in the 1890s?
questions.fact: They ran a health sanitarium in Michigan. Their first flakes, reportedly from cooked wheat left standing, were made of wheat, not corn.

questions.question: How was the ice lolly reportedly invented in 1905?
options: A chef dropped juice on ice
A boy left a drink out overnight
questions.fact: By his own account, 11-year-old Frank Epperson left soda with a stirring stick outside on a cold night. He patented the idea in 1924.

questions.question: Which French brothers' hot-air balloon carried the first human passengers, in 1783?
questions.fact: Before risking people, they sent up a sheep, a duck and a rooster in front of King Louis XVI at Versailles.

questions.question: The Lumière brothers are famous for pioneering what?
questions.fact: Their first public paid film screening was held in a Paris café in December 1895, showing ten short films.

questions.question: Which discovery reportedly happened when Charles Goodyear dropped rubber mixed with sulphur onto a hot stove?
questions.fact: The Goodyear tyre company was named in his honour decades after his death. He had no link to it and died deep in debt.

questions.question: Engineer Martin Cooper made the first handheld mobile phone call in 1973 for which company?
questions.fact: Cooper reportedly called a rival at Bell Labs to tell him. The prototype weighed about 1.1 kg.

questions.question: Which everyday item did King Camp Gillette make famous in the early 1900s?
questions.fact: Sales took off during World War I, when the US Army issued Gillette razors to its soldiers.

questions.question: Which famous rain boots are named after a British duke?
questions.fact: The first Duke of Wellington had his shoemaker adapt a style of leather boot. Rubber "wellies" came later, after vulcanised rubber.

questions.question: Which British engineer invented the bagless "cyclone" vacuum cleaner?
questions.fact: By his own account, Dyson built 5,127 prototypes over about five years before he got the design right.

questions.question: Which company launched the Walkman portable cassette player in 1979?
questions.fact: Sony co-founder Masaru Ibuka reportedly wanted a way to listen to opera on his long business flights.

questions.question: Which red pocket tool did Karl Elsener start making for soldiers in 1891?
questions.fact: His company is now Victorinox. The English name reportedly came from American soldiers after WWII who found "Offiziersmesser" hard to say.
